name: Puruhutika Devi and Kukkuteswara Swamy Temple, Pithapuram
nativeName: శ్రీ పురుహూతికా దేవి – కుక్కుటేశ్వర స్వామి ఆలయం, పిఠాపురం
deity: The Goddess as Puruhutika, within the temple of Shiva as Kukkuteswara with Rajarajeswari
period: An ancient pilgrimage centre — the Pishtapura of early inscriptions — and one of the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas
dynasty: Traditional; Pithapuram was an early seat of the Eastern Chalukyas
summary: In the old town of Pithapuram, the goddess Puruhutika is worshipped as one of the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas within the temple of Kukkuteswara, beside the Pada Gaya tank where pilgrims offer rites for their ancestors.

sections.history: Pithapuram, near the coast of the Godavari delta, is among the oldest towns of Andhra: as Pishtapura it appears in Samudragupta's fourth-century inscription at Prayaga, and in the seventh century it served as an early seat of the Eastern Chalukyas before they moved to Vengi. Its great temple is dedicated to Shiva as Kukkuteswara Swamy, and within the same complex the goddess Puruhutika has her shrine, counted among the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas named in the hymn attributed to Adi Shankara. Together with its sacred tank, the Pada Gaya, the temple has drawn pilgrims for centuries, both to seek the goddess's grace and to perform rites for departed ancestors, which are held here to be as meritorious as those offered at Gaya or Kashi.
sections.architecture: The temple is a walled Dravidian complex, with the sanctum of Kukkuteswara at its heart. The linga is held to be self-manifested, and devotees see in its form the shape of a rooster, the kukkuta that gives the lord his name; Rajarajeswari is worshipped as his consort. The shrine of Puruhutika Devi stands within the same enclosure, and before the complex lies the broad Pada Gaya tank, its steps worn by generations of bathers. Large footprints near the flagstaff are shown to pilgrims as those of Gayasura.
sections.legends: Pithapuram joins two great sacred stories. As a Shakti Peetha it belongs to the legend of Sati, whose body, carried by the grieving Shiva, fell in parts across the land; tradition holds that her seat fell here. The tank recalls Gayasura, a devotee whose body was so vast that his head lay at Gaya, his navel at Jajpur and his feet at Pithapuram — hence Pada Gaya, the 'Gaya of the feet'. A local tale adds that Shiva crowed as a rooster to bring his long penance to a close, and remained here as Kukkuteswara.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the great festival of Kukkuteswara, and Navaratri is celebrated with special worship of Puruhutika Devi. The month of Karthika brings bathers to the Pada Gaya and lamps to the temple, and ancestral rites are performed at the tank through the year, especially on new-moon days. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Pilgrims usually bathe or sprinkle water at the Pada Gaya, worship Kukkuteswara and Rajarajeswari, and then seek the darshan of Puruhutika Devi. The town is also cherished by followers of the Dattatreya tradition as the birthplace of Sripada Srivallabha, whose shrine lies nearby. The temples of the Godavari delta, including Draksharamam and Annavaram, make natural companions.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan and a midday closure; Shivaratri, Navaratri and Karthika are busiest. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Those performing ancestral rites at the tank are guided by the local priests.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted in the sanctums; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Pithapuram lies about 20 km from Kakinada and has a railway station on the Vijayawada–Visakhapatnam main line. The nearest airports are at Rajahmundry and Visakhapatnam, with good road connections along the coast.
